paragraphs.source_en: Lastly, I should like to say a word about the exercise I call “making the round of the fence.” My master’s garden is enclosed in a rectangle by a bamboo fence; the side parallel to the veranda must be five or six jo long, while the fences on the left and right are only about two jo four shaku each. The exercise I now call “making the round of the fence” consists of going once around the top of this bamboo fence without falling off. I often come to grief at this exercise, but when it succeeds it is highly entertaining. Especially convenient is the fact that, at no great intervals, wooden posts stand along the fence and provide me with brief resting places. Today I was in rather good form; from morning till noon I had done it three times, and each attempt was cleverer than the last. The cleverer I became, the more interested I grew. At last I attempted it a fourth time. On that fourth round, when I had made it about halfway along the bamboo fence, three crows flew over from the neighbor’s roof and perched in a neat row five or six shaku ahead of me. What insolent fellows, arriving uninvited for the express purpose of obstructing another’s exercise! Worse still, they were of unknown origin, without so much as a household register, and yet they had the effrontery to fly onto another’s garden wall as they pleased. Was there ever anything so outrageous? Thinking thus, I called out to them, “Hey! I am coming through. Move aside!” The foremost crow looked over at me and grinned. The second crow stared fixedly into my master’s garden. The third kept wiping its beak on the bamboo of the fence; they must certainly have come after eating something. To await their answer, I allowed them three minutes for consideration and remained standing on the wall. Crows are commonly nicknamed Kanzaburo, and true to the name, after all that time they neither flew away nor gave me any reply. Having no alternative, I began to move slowly forward; then the Kanzaburo perched in front gave a small flap of its wings. I thought it had at last been overawed by my majesty and was about to flee, but no: it merely turned its head from right to left and changed its posture. The scoundrel! Were we on the ground, I would certainly not let it off lightly. But alas, this exercise of “making the round of the fence” is hard enough as it is, and I had no leisure to quarrel with Kanzaburo; yet, on the other hand, I was not inclined to stand there waiting for the three crows to move aside. To begin with, if I waited like that my legs would give out. They are creatures with wings and can remain perched here; consequently, if it pleases them, they may stay indefinitely. As for me, this was already my fourth round of the fence today, and I was tired enough even without this trouble. Moreover, I was engaged in an act of performance and exercise more difficult than tightrope walking. Even with no obstacle at all I could not guarantee I would not fall, and now three fellows dressed entirely in black were blocking my way; it was an exceedingly awkward predicament. If matters came to the worst, I would have no choice but to climb down from the wall and suspend the exercise. To avoid further trouble, I thought I might as well do just that.

paragraphs.source_zh: 最后，我想讲讲“绕竹墙”的运动。主人的院子是用竹篱笆围成长方形的，和廊子平行的那面篱笆足有五六丈长，但左右两侧的篱笆只不过各有两丈四尺长。如今，我所说的“绕竹墙”运动，是指在这竹篱笆顶上绕行一周而不掉下来。这个运动，我经常搞失败，但如果做成功了，倒是很有乐趣。特别是隔不太远的篱笆上就立有一根木桩子，给我提供了稍事休息的便利。今天我的功夫做得比较好，从清晨到中午，已经做了三遍，一遍比一遍做得巧妙。越是巧妙越有兴致。终于我又做了第四遍。在做第四遍的时候，我刚在竹篱笆上绕行了一半，邻居的屋顶飞来了三只乌鸦，在我五六尺的前方整齐地排列着。这是一群不请自来的家伙，专来妨碍人家的运动！尤其是它们来历不明，连个户籍也没有，居然随便飞到人家的院墙上来，真是岂有此理？我想到这里，便向它们喊道：“喂！我要过去，躲开！”最前边的那只乌鸦朝我这边嘻嘻地笑着。第二只乌鸦死盯着主人的院子。第三只则在竹篱笆上反复擦它的嘴，它们肯定是吃过什么东西以后才来的。我为了等待它们的答复，给了它们三分钟的考虑时间，一直站在墙上。乌鸦的诨名称做“勘左卫门”，果然不愧是勘左卫门，我等了那么久，它们既不飞走，也不搭话。我不得已只好缓慢地向前走去，这时，停在最前边的勘左卫门，扑扇了一下翅膀。我以为它们总算畏惧我的威势要逃走了，哪想到它只是把头从右向左转，只改变了一下姿势而已。这混蛋！若是在地上，我决不会轻饶它。无奈我这“绕竹墙”的运动本来就十分费劲儿，根本没有工夫去和勘左卫门怄气，可话又说回来，我又不情愿停在那里等待这三只乌鸦躲开。首先，这样等下去我的腿就发软了。对方是有翅膀的东西，能够继续停在这里，因而只要它们高兴，就可以无限期地逗留下去。而我呢，今天已经是第四次做“绕竹墙”运动，即使不遇上这个麻烦也够累的了。更何况我在搞比走钢丝还困难的表演兼运动呢。即使没有任何障碍物还难保不摔下去，可偏遇上三个穿得满身乌黑的家伙挡路，这真是件令我极其犯难的事儿。实在不行，我只好从墙头上下来停止这项运动。为了避免惹麻烦，我想干脆就如此行动吧。
